content: The study conducted by Dr. Emily A. Kendall, MD, PhD, focused on evaluating the economic implications of changes in treatment regimens for multidrug-resistant or rifampin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB). These changes could influence drug costs, drug delivery methods (e.g., injections), safety monitoring requirements, follow-up visits, and the number of future TB patients requiring treatment due to improved or worsened treatment outcomes. The study aimed to assess whether these changes would result in cost savings or increased costs, weighing these economic factors against potential clinical benefits. A decision-analytic model was developed to estimate the costs and cost-effectiveness of three potential changes to recommended MDR/RR-TB treatment regimens. The analysis was conducted for adult patients with pulmonary MDR/RR-TB (excluding pre-XDR or XDR-TB cases). The model incorporated data on treatment outcomes, including relapse, failure, mortality, and loss to follow-up, based on statistical analyses of individual patient data. For the first scenario (PICO 1), a shorter (9–12 months), all-oral, bedaquiline-containing regimen was compared to two currently recommended regimens: (a) a longer (18–20 months), all-oral regimen containing bedaquiline, linezolid, levofloxacin, clofazimine, and terizidone, and (b) a shorter (9–12 months) regimen that included injectable drugs. The shorter all-oral regimen was projected to be cost-saving compared to both alternatives, with savings of approximately $3,000 per patient compared to the longer all-oral regimen and $1,000 per patient compared to the shorter injectable-containing regimen. These savings were primarily attributed to reduced drug costs, healthcare delivery costs, adverse event management, and future retreatment costs. Additionally, the shorter all-oral regimen was projected to be more effective than either comparator. For the third scenario (PICO 3), extending the duration of bedaquiline treatment from six months to the full 18–20 months of a longer all-oral regimen was estimated to increase health system costs by approximately $500 per patient. The cost-effectiveness of this extension depended heavily on the magnitude of the clinical benefit. While extending bedaquiline treatment might be cost-effective for select patients with high-risk profiles, the available data did not demonstrate a sufficiently large benefit to justify its use for all patients. For the fourth scenario (PICO 4), the concurrent use of delamanid and bedaquiline was evaluated. Delamanid was modeled either as an addition to the longer all-oral regimen (to potentially increase efficacy) or as a replacement for linezolid (to reduce toxicity). However, the high cost of delamanid made achieving cost-effectiveness challenging. Even under optimistic assumptions about its efficacy, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was $2,000 per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted in South Africa. In less favorable scenarios, the addition of delamanid resulted in increased costs without significant clinical benefit. A qualitative study was also conducted to explore patient perspectives on MDR/XDR-TB treatment. Patients expressed a strong preference for treatment regimens that minimized disruption to their daily lives and allowed for full physical and mental recovery. The most acceptable regimens were short, injection-free, had minimal side effects, and required a low pill burden. Severe and persistent side effects, such as vomiting, mental health issues (e.g., severe depression or anxiety), and organ or sensory damage (e.g., hearing or vision loss), were deemed unacceptable. Patients emphasized the importance of informed choice in treatment decisions and highlighted the need for equitable access to new drugs and regimens, particularly in remote or underserved areas. In conclusion, the study found that a 9–12 month all-oral regimen was both cost-saving and effective compared to longer or injectable-containing regimens. However, extending bedaquiline treatment or adding delamanid to longer regimens incurred substantial costs and were unlikely to be cost-effective at current drug prices when applied universally. These findings underscore the importance of patient-centered approaches and equitable access to treatment in the development of MDR/RR-TB treatment guidelines.
